intro: The Ninth’s Rondo-Burleske makes the whole orchestra a virtuoso, with jagged tunes elbowing past one another at speed. In the middle, a trumpet sings a D-major melody that the finale will remember.

sections.label: A · Trumpet calls and jagged strings
sections.mNote: Short figures combine into the rondo’s competing lines

sections.label: B · A trumpet sings in D major
sections.mNote: Held strings support a melody with a small turning figure

sections.label: B′ · Harp sweeps and tremolos
sections.mNote: Harp sweeps and string tremolos separate the sharp replies

sections.label: A′ · The rondo returns
sections.mNote: The opening figures return and drive towards the close

sections.label: Coda · Più stretto, then Presto
sections.mNote: Short orchestral figures drive towards an abrupt A-minor close

cues.title: A trumpet starts a fight
cues.text: A solo trumpet throws out a short figure, and Mahler marks the movement Allegro assai. Sehr trotzig — very defiant. Strings answer with jagged figures; horns and woodwinds add short ones of their own. Then the violins take up the main melody at ff, a tune that keeps arguing with itself.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, Universal Edition first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 104: Allegro assai. Sehr trotzig; first trumpet alone in the first bar, string, horn and woodwind figures, the violins’ melody ff. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: chromatic fragments in the brass introduce the refrain, sehr trotzig, and the violins then take up the main melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: To my brothers in Apollo
cues.text: Mahler dedicates the movement, with a sneer, “to my brothers in Apollo”: his fellow disciples of the god of music.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik’s note for Universal Edition describes the Rondo-Burleske as derisively dedicated to my brothers in Apollo: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Mahler-Symphony-No.-9-Original-draft-of-1st-3-Movements.-Facsimile-of-Composers-Manuscript-D-major-for-orchestra/P0005537

cues.title: A tune out strolling
cues.text: The first episode lightens the tone: smaller forces, softer dynamics, one flat in the key signature, and melodies with the swing of operetta. The rondo’s dissonance is still there underneath.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 111–114: one flat, reduced scoring. Basinger: the first episode keeps the refrain’s dissonance and some of its contrapuntal sophistication, but the reduced scoring and softer dynamic level brighten the tone, and the melodic lines channel the style of operetta and other popular music of the period: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna before the Anschluss
cues.text: This performance takes place in January 1938. Two months later, Nazi Germany annexes Austria. Walter, already driven from Germany because he is Jewish, must leave his adopted country too; Mahler’s music disappears from its concert programmes.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, p. 2, on the recording, Anschluss, Walter’s exile and suppression of Mahler’s music. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: A muted trumpet calls
cues.text: A muted trumpet calls out twice, ff and fading at once, while a triangle roll swells and the violins churn on repeated notes.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 123: first trumpet mit Dämpfer, ff dim.; triangle roll with crescendo; violins on repeated notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Counterpoint, in Walter’s words
cues.text: In 1936 Bruno Walter called this movement “defiantly agitated” and found in it “most striking proof” of Mahler’s contrapuntal mastery.
cues.evidence: Walter’s Gustav Mahler (1936), quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: The trumpet starts to sing
cues.text: A cymbal stroke halts the fugue. Brass chords sound a dissonant chorale, and then, at Etwas gehalten, D major arrives: a solo trumpet, marked p subito poco espressivo, sings a gentle melody over trembling strings. That little turn will return in the finale.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 132: Beck. stroke, flutes Flatterzunge, brass chords, Etwas gehalten, two sharps, trumpet p subito poco espressivo over string tremolo pp subito. Basinger: a cymbal crash halts the imitative process, the second episode begins with a dissonant chorale from the preceding fugue and then a lyrical melody full of turn motives and sigh figures; the finale’s primary melody absorbs the turn motive of the Rondo-Burleske: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bewildered refugee in Paris
cues.text: A few weeks after the concert, Fred Gaisberg meets Walter in Paris to play him the test pressings: “a bewildered refugee”. Walter is “so delighted” with the results that his “usually sober face brightened up considerably”.
cues.evidence: Gaisberg’s 1944 account, quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: Harp sweeps clear the stage
cues.text: Scraps of the rondo keep creeping into the song, and each time a harp glissando sweeps them away, leaving the violins trembling am Steg, near the bridge, in divided parts.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 141: harp glissandos, second violins 3fach geteilt, am Steg, pp, immer Dämpfer in the horns.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song is turned away
cues.text: The mood darkens. The oboe, and then other instruments, keep trying to bring the lyrical melody back, but the orchestra rejects it, and the rondo’s fragments creep back.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the mood darkens as a clarinet gruffly anticipates the refrain; the oboe, followed by other instruments, keeps trying to reinstate the lyrical melody, and the orchestra ultimately rejects it: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: Faster, then faster again
cues.text: Più stretto, then Presto: the closing pages tighten the screw. Winds, brass and strings repeat the opening’s short figures with fierce accents. The movement ends on the same kind of sharp call that set it going.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 157–163: Più stretto on p. 157, short repeated figures in winds, brass and strings at ff, final short attacks on p. 163. Basinger: the refrain resurfaces and the Rondo-Burleske ends in the same ill-humour in which it opened: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A cymbal crash, then D major
transitions.from: A · Trumpet calls and jagged strings
transitions.to: B · A trumpet sings in D major
transitions.how: A cymbal stroke clears away the crowded lines. Flutter-tongued flutes and trembling strings hold on, brass chords sound a dissonant chorale, and at Etwas gehalten the harmony settles into D major under a solo trumpet.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 132. Basinger: a cymbal crash halts the imitative process; a dissonant chorale precedes the lyrical melody.

transitions.title: A harp glissando clears the scraps
transitions.from: B · A trumpet sings in D major
transitions.how: The broad melody falls apart into replies. Scraps of the rondo break in, and a harp glissando sweeps them away, restoring the quiet string tremolo, am Steg.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 141: harp glissandos, string tremolo am Steg pp.

transitions.title: The short figures accelerate
transitions.how: The repeated figures press into Più stretto and later Presto. Strings, winds and brass crowd the short opening motifs together, with percussion reinforcing their accents. The final A-minor attacks cut off the rush.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 157–163, tempo markings and final A-minor chords.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement III, printed pp. 104–163: opening trumpet call; D-major trumpet melody in the central episode; E♭-clarinet interruptions; accelerating close on pp. 157–163.

timeline.note: A solo trumpet gives the first short call before the strings answer.
Jagged string figures and horn calls cross rising lines in winds and low strings.
The solo trumpet sings in D major above held, trembling strings.
Clarinets sharpen the melody’s turn; harp sweeps interrupt the returning rondo fragments.
Trombones and low strings restore the opening theme.
Short figures race through the orchestra, with timpani and percussion reinforcing the accents.

fields.note: The recording sources identify the complete movement but do not establish the performing edition or any local alterations. The 1912 full score is used as a structural reference, not proof of the parts on the 1938 desks.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

fields.label: Recording rights

fields.note: The inspected template expressly concerns expired performer and producer rights in the European Union. This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
